strategies.plan:
Mechanism family: slope-directed-marginal-reassignment (new; local exploitation role; distinct from bottleneck-ejection/offload families which used ejection chains and repair, not marginal-slope ordering)
Replacement scope: replace `_local_search` (the hill climber) with a slope-directed descent; it is called from the same sites in `compute_model_placement` and `_anneal` remains as escape.
Compute budget: each descent is O(iterations × n × g) with iterations bounded by n·g (each accepted move strictly reduces max KVPR, so at most the number of distinct KVPR values is visited); replaces the existing local search cost, net runtime change ≈ 0.
Gain mechanism: the incumbent hill climber accepts any move that lowers the max KVPR, taking the *first* found improvement, which often trades a large bottleneck reduction for a near-tie that leaves the new bottleneck barely below the old one — it gets stuck at "staircase" local optima. The new degree of freedom: for the current argmax GPU g*, enumerate all (model, target GPU) moves and all swaps involving g*, and rank them by the *resulting second-highest KVPR*, i.e., minimize max(new_kvpr(g*), max over other GPUs) with a tie-break on the margin (new_max vs second_max gap) — choosing moves that maximize slack, not just the immediate max. Additionally allow "plateau walks": moves that keep max KVPR exactly equal (within 1e-12) but reduce the *sum* of KVPRs, which the incumbent forbids; plateau walks are the escape route from staircase optima that strict descent cannot traverse. Memory feasibility is checked before every move (mem[g] + size < GPU_MEM_SIZE), and the best-ever snapshot is kept so the function never returns worse than its input.
Expected-gain check: the incumbent local search cannot traverse zero-width plateaus (it requires strict improvement > 1e-12), so any instance where the optimum sits across a plateau is unreachable for it; this strategy adds exactly that move class, with the falsifiable threshold that on the fixed test suite the raw max-KVPR average drops strictly below the incumbent's (score > 26.255972) whenever any plateau exists, and is unchanged otherwise.
